title: What are the common microservices anti-patterns and their fixes: over-splitting (start with a modular monolith), chatty services (BFF/aggregation), the "god gateway" (keep business logic out of the gateway), retry storms/thundering herd (backoff + jitter + circuit breaker + retry budgets), tight coupling via shared libraries (share contracts, not code), and no service ownership?
shortTitle: What are the common microservices anti-patterns and their fixes?
keyPoints: Over-splitting: too many tiny services before boundaries are clear; fix by starting with a modular monolith.
Chatty services: one request triggers many fine-grained network calls; fix with a BFF or aggregation layer.
God gateway: business logic stuffed into the API gateway; fix by keeping the gateway limited to cross-cutting concerns.
Retry storms: naive retries amplify an outage; fix with exponential backoff, jitter, circuit breakers, and retry budgets.
Shared-library coupling: domain code in a common library forces lockstep deploys; fix by sharing contracts not code.
No service ownership: no team is accountable; fix with clear single-team ownership (you build it, you run it).
Most anti-patterns come from adopting microservices prematurely or partially.

s1_definition.oneliner: The common microservices anti-patterns -- over-splitting, chatty services, god gateway, retry storms, shared-library coupling, and no ownership -- each reintroduce the pain microservices should remove, and each has a standard fix.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Over-splitting** – too many tiny services before boundaries are understood; fix: start with a modular monolith.
- **Chatty services** – one request triggers many fine-grained calls; fix: BFF or aggregation layer.
- **God gateway** – business logic in the API gateway; fix: keep the gateway thin (auth, rate limiting, routing only).
- **Retry storms** – naive retries amplify outages; fix: backoff + jitter + circuit breakers + retry budgets.
- **Shared-library coupling** – domain code in a shared library forces lockstep deploys; fix: share contracts, not code.
- **No ownership** – nobody maintains the service; fix: you-build-it-you-run-it with service catalog.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India trips over the same mistakes repeatedly. Over-splitting is giving every clerk their own office building. Chatty services is the loan desk phoning five other desks instead of getting one combined report. A god gateway is the security guard trying to approve loans himself. Retry storms are a hundred anxious customers all redialing the same busy number. Shared-library coupling is every department re-issuing its entire rulebook for one rule change. No ownership is a department everyone uses but nobody fixes.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Microservices Anti-Patterns and Fixes

  Over-splitting          → Modular Monolith first
  ┌─┐ ┌─┐ ┌─┐ ┌─┐ ┌─┐     ┌──────────────┐
  │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │  →  │ Monolith     │
  └─┘ └─┘ └─┘ └─┘ └─┘     │ with modules │
  too many services         └──────────────┘

  Chatty Services          → BFF Aggregation
  Client ─→ A              Client ─→ BFF ─→ A,B,C,D
         ─→ B                        (1 call, parallel)
         ─→ C
         ─→ D
  4 round trips             1 round trip

  Retry Storm              → Backoff + Budget
  100 clients × 3 retries  100 clients × budget cap
  = 300 calls (amplify!)   = 110 calls (bounded)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The common microservices anti-patterns each reintroduce the very pain microservices should remove. Over-splitting creates too many services before boundaries are clear, so a feature becomes a cross-service coordination project. Chatty services make one request trigger many fine-grained calls, ballooning latency. The god gateway stuffs business logic into the API gateway, making it a shared bottleneck. Retry storms pile naive retries onto a struggling service, amplifying the outage. Shared-library coupling forces lockstep deploys. No ownership lets services rot.

The fixes are standard. Start with a modular monolith and extract only when needed. Aggregate with a BFF so one client call fans out server-side. Keep the gateway thin. Use backoff with jitter, circuit breakers, and retry budgets. Share contracts not code. Assign one accountable team per service.

At National Bank of India, Pankaj fixed a chatty mobile dashboard with a BFF that aggregated account, card, and rewards into one call, and tamed a retry storm with backoff, jitter, a circuit breaker, and a retry budget so a slow rewards service no longer collapsed the dashboard path.

Remember one sentence: the microservices anti-patterns are over-splitting, chatty services, god gateway, retry storms, shared-library coupling, and no ownership, and the fixes are modular monolith first, BFF aggregation, thin gateway, backoff with budgets, contracts not code, and one team per service.
